title: Wild Chase Dylan Larkin: Do They Have the Assets to Pull Off the Blockbuster Deal?
body:
The Minnesota Wild have thrown their weight behind a trade for Detroit’s former captain Dylan Larkin, but the price tag required to bring the dynamic forward to the Upper Midwest may force the franchise to enlist a third‑party partner to close the deal. As the deadline looms, General Manager Bill Guerin and his scouting staff are weighing a package that could include prospects, draft picks and possibly a player from another organization, underscoring the difficulty of acquiring a top‑tier center in a market where assets are already thin.

Larkin, who was drafted 15th overall by the Red Wings in 2012 and spent his entire professional career in Detroit, has been the subject of relentless speculation since his contract expired this summer. His agent, Pat Brisson, confirmed that the 28‑year‑old is open to a move, citing a desire for a fresh challenge and a more competitive roster. The Wild, who have hovered around the playoff bubble for the past two seasons, view Larkin as the missing piece to elevate their offense and provide a true number‑one center alongside Joel Eriksson‑Ekström and Jordan Greenway. In return, Detroit expects a return that reflects Larkin’s proven scoring ability—approximately 30 goals and 70 points per season at his peak.

The Wild’s current inventory makes a straight‑up exchange problematic. Minnesota’s farm system boasts a handful of promising forwards, such as forward‑center prospect Anton Miller and defenseman Joonas Laitinen, but none match the caliber of a former captain with Larkin’s pedigree. Their 2025 first‑round pick, a valuable commodity in a draft class featuring several elite forwards, could be part of the equation, yet surrendering it would hamper the franchise’s long‑term rebuilding plan. Moreover, Minnesota’s salary cap situation is already tight after committing to a new contract for forward Matt Boldy and retaining several veteran deals.

Because of these constraints, insiders suggest that a three‑team trade may be the most viable route. The Chicago Blackhawks, who sit deep in the cap and possess a surplus of mid‑level contracts, could act as a conduit, sending a player such as forward Mason McDonald to Detroit in exchange for a pick that would then be packaged to Minnesota. This type of triangular deal has precedent in recent NHL history, most notably the 2022 trade that sent Auston Matthews to Toronto via a third team. The involvement of a third club would allow each participant to address specific roster needs while distributing the financial burden more evenly.

Analysts caution that even a three‑team structure may not satisfy Detroit’s demands. The Red Wings have signaled they are looking to accelerate their rebuild by acquiring multiple high‑end assets, not just a single first‑rounder. A package that includes a second‑round pick, a prospect like forward Jasper Miller, and a depth forward could be the minimum acceptable return. If Minnesota cannot meet those expectations, the trade could collapse, leaving Larkin to test free agency—a scenario that would likely see him sign with a contender willing to meet his market value.

The clock is ticking, and the Wild’s front office appears prepared to make bold moves. Should they secure Larkin, Minnesota would instantly upgrade its top‑line chemistry, providing a playmaking hub that could translate into a deeper playoff run. Conversely, failing to close the deal may force the Wild to explore alternative options, such as targeting other available centers or doubling down on internal development. As the trade deadline approaches, the league will watch closely to see whether Minnesota can marshal the necessary assets—or a willing partner—to finally bring Dylan Larkin home.
